findings.reason: The authenticated schema explicitly allows duplicate UserActivity rows while also prohibiting simultaneous activities. Exact copies therefore carry one logical period, but the protected query ranks raw storage rows. Two copies of the newest period occupy ranks one and two and cause the query to return the newest activity instead of the preceding logical activity. The candidate deduplicates all four source columns before applying the same window-ranking method.

DISTINCT maps every set of identical storage rows to one logical activity period. Nonoverlap then makes descending startDate an unambiguous chronology per user. ROW_NUMBER assigns rank two to exactly the second newest period, partition COUNT identifies exactly the one-period fallback, and the filter returns one complete source row per user. Omitting a final sort respects the source's unrestricted result order.

Protected and native queries pass the exact source example, seven of eight visible cases, and every benchmark output, but return the duplicated newest row instead of the middle row in the duplicate-newest trial. They also disagreed with the independent logical-period oracle on 4,212 of 5,000 randomized source-valid databases. Their exact bytes and verified submission evidence were preserved; the fix exists only as an inert candidate.

An independent Python oracle deduplicated exact four-field tuples, partitioned them by username, ordered each partition by startDate, and selected its second newest or sole row. It, the candidate, a separately written GROUP BY plus window control, and a correct slower correlated-count control agreed as unordered row multisets on all eight visible cases, all three benchmark tiers, and every randomized database.

Seed 1369 generated 5,000 source-valid databases with 208,723 stored rows representing 146,021 logical periods. Coverage included 4,913 databases with duplicate rows, 4,568 with several users, 13,072 user partitions with a duplicated newest period, 4,060 single-period partitions, 4,103 two-period partitions, 25,116 partitions with repeated activity names on different dates, nonoverlapping periods, and shuffled storage order; candidate and controls matched the oracle throughout.

Across three real-test repetitions, the candidate passed all eight ordinary cases, all three benchmark outputs, and scaling with extra growth exponent -0.08 through -0.03 and largest-tier ratio 1.11x through 1.15x. The independent grouped-window control passed at +0.01 through +0.04 and 1.14x through 1.16x. The de-indexed correlated count passed every output but failed only scaling each time, at +0.72 through +0.77 relative exponent and 7.21x through 7.73x largest-tier ratio.

All three benchmark cases remain explicitly hidden and performance-only, use positive unique sizes 16, 64, and 256 for a 16x span, and define size consistently as stored UserActivity rows. Four chronological activities per user require partitioning and second-newest selection across 4/16/64 users. Candidate and an independent optimal-class control pass repeatedly while the correct per-row correlated scans fail only growth, so benchmark.json was not edited.

The complete Approach now targets the candidate and derives duplicate normalization from the duplicate-row and nonoverlap clauses before explaining partition ranks and the single-period fallback. It proves one-row-per-user correctness, states O(A log A) time and O(A) space, and covers raw-row ranking failure, correlated and two-maximum alternatives, one and two periods, duplicates, arbitrary input/output order, multiple users, and source-row integrity.

All eight ordinary cases are visible samples or trials and use unordered-table validation. The sole authenticated example is restored exactly with Alice's three dated activities, Bob's sole Travel row, both source outputs, and the complete explanation. Two invented samples were relabeled as trials, former hidden cases are visible, and a duplicate-newest trial now covers the explicit duplicate-row contract and exposes the protected defect.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode database problem 1369 and SQL/MySQL as the native environment. The candidate respects duplicate storage rows, nonoverlapping logical periods, per-user chronology, the second-newest rule, the sole-activity fallback, all four selected source columns, one result per user, and unrestricted output order.

The protected app-local sql.sql and immutable leetcode.sql bound to verified submission 2068748473 remain byte-for-byte identical and unchanged, as does submission.json. solution_variants.json continues to select the protected source; candidate.sql is separate and inert, with no remote-Accepted status inferred or recorded for it.

A fresh authenticated Premium review confirmed the four-column UserActivity schema, allowed duplicate rows, activity-period meaning, second-most-recent task, sole-activity fallback, no-simultaneous-activity guarantee, unrestricted output order, one exact example with its full explanation, three source tables, and no constraints, hints, notes, images, diagrams, or follow-up. source_fidelity.json binds four modular Reference files to live-content SHA-256 e705dd684f5695250ded1d3acc3c81c19494d1cc8b36f3e2def7567f585e5192 and validates without errors.
